title: Narrative Snippets: Writing for Story Games (Failbetter)
rule: Text read repeatedly must be shortest: one sentence for root/branch descriptions, one paragraph for event text; lead with the important thing because players skim after the second read; avoid semicolons/parentheses; success text slightly longer or more interesting than failure text; past four or five paragraphs is too far.
example: "a single sentence for root and branch descriptions and a paragraph for event text will do fine"; "shove the important stuff at them straight away"; "Economy of prose is a virtue."

title: Points of light, pools of shadow (part II) (Failbetter)
rule: Plain, unobtrusive vocabulary (says, not utters); period flavour as a few deliberate touches, not pastiche of real Victorian prose; almost never write the player's own words; minor characters get generic titles, only central ones get names (fewer continuity problems); write lines that fit many player histories; break the rules when a scene earns it.
example: "Says rather than utters." / "Shouts, not vociferises." / "We (almost) never put words directly into the player's mouth." / "Whatever happened between us in the past, business is business." / "Characters without individual names are more universal, less specific, less prone to continuity problems."

title: Narrative Snippets: Agency and Choices (Failbetter)
rule: Prefer a series of small two-option choices to one large menu; never re-offer the choice just made; record choices as qualities but keep reactive content per quality small (combinatorial explosion); acknowledge past choices only occasionally; split a big decision into a situation storylet then a choice storylet; do not narrate the player's feelings in option or result text.
example: "It's usually better to present a series of five two-option choices rather than give ten options" (summarizer flagged this as a paraphrase); "having a lot can lead to Combinatorial Explosion, which you want to avoid"

title: Fallen London Writer Guidelines, Part II: Designing for Fallen London
rule: Design not prose rules: minimise new qualities (two is the working minimum); write notes for a stranger a year later; batch rewards at the end of a strand; include reminders in content for sporadic players; use [square-bracket advisory text] for explicit guidance; a string of quality changes in one result makes each less important.
example: "Provide reminders in content so players can reorient themselves." / "Use [advisory text in square brackets] to provide the player with emphasised, explicit guidance and warnings." / "a string of quality changes in a result makes each one less important."

title: Fallen London Writer Guidelines, Part I: Pitching
rule: Process only, no prose rules: pitch with business case, theme, size in storylets; skeleton playable before prose; write the prose last; the writer must play the content through in-game before QA; register new characters/places/lore in a shared spreadsheet.
example: "you must have played through it yourself, in-game, from beginning to end."

title: GDC 2012 talk on dynamic dialogue (Emily Short summarising Elan Ruskin)

title: Using item flavor to tell stories (search snippet; fetch returned HTTP 500)
rule: Item text carries story: point to origin, a famous former owner or a historical event rather than stating mechanics; Souls games convey a deep world with little exposition because curious players read every item description and infer the rest. A separate promotional generator page (thestoryshack.com, low reliability, snippet only) adds: name a previous wielder or a binding vow rather than the stat, end on an image not a number, trim any sentence that over-explains. No verbatim shipped example obtained.

title: Thoughts for prospective IFComp authors? (intfiction forum)
rule: Reviewer-side complaints: bugs and typos are the top irritant; do not apologise for flaws in the blurb; endings can sink a whole game; blurb should convey tone and genre like a product description; keep to roughly a two-hour play budget. Nothing found on prose-length or choice-text rules.
example: "Bugs and typos are strongly frowned upon." / "A walkthrough that's just a string of commands can be very disorienting."

title: Wildermyth lays bare the false promises of AI storytelling (Superjump)
read: full (via fetch summarizer; critical essay, not craft guide)
rule: Procedural scenes are hand-written scripts with variable inputs (party relationships, personalities, past events), plus alternate scripts per outcome; writers wrote without knowing who the characters would be. No line-level rules recoverable.
example: "the scenario is pre-written, but it will change slightly each time depending on the characters in your party"
